title: Log Enumeration
summary: Log enumeration is the reading, exporting, or continuous monitoring of logs on a compromised host or logging platform in order to learn about the environment and about the defenders. An adversary may query the Windows event log with wevtutil or through PowerShell, export security events to a file, or, in cloud environments, pull guest logs through an agent utility, and may then send the collection to their own infrastructure for offline review. The value runs in two directions. Historically the logs reveal authentication records, installed software, and other hosts, which feeds account, software, and remote system discovery. Increasingly they also expose the incident response itself: an attacker watching authentication or administrative events in real time can see when defenders notice and adjust accordingly. Detection rests on auditing the audit, meaning process creation records for the querying tools, event log access or clearing events, and unusual read volumes against a central log store.

beginner.definition: Logs are records that computers keep about what happened. Enumerating logs means reading through them to find useful facts. Attackers do this to learn about your network and to see whether anyone has noticed them.
beginner.whyItMatters: Your logs hold a map of your environment: who logs in, which software runs, and which systems exist. In the wrong hands, that map saves the attacker a lot of guesswork. Worse, they can watch the logs to see when defenders start investigating. That lets them hide or change tactics before they are caught. If you never watch who reads your logs, you lose that advantage.
howItWorks: The attacker gains access to a host or to an account that can read log data.
They use built in tools to query or export the system and security logs.
They search the results for user accounts, login records, and installed software.
They look for other machines and services that could be reached next.
Sometimes they copy the logs out to their own systems for slower review.
They may keep watching live logs to see when defenders begin to react.
beginner.example: Imagine a warehouse office with a sign in book on the desk. It lists every driver who came in, what they collected, and which gate they used. A thief who gets into the office at night does not just take stock. They read the book. Now they know the delivery times, the quiet hours, and the names of the staff on shift. On later visits they keep an eye on the book. That way they can tell whether the manager has started asking questions. Log enumeration is reading that book. The records meant to protect the warehouse, and instead they became a guide for the intruder.
takeaways: Logs are intelligence for defenders and for attackers alike.
Alert on bulk log reads, exports, and log clearing, not only on failed logins.
Limit who can read central logs, and record every access to them.

objectives: Explain why an attacker reads system and security logs.
Name the Windows tools commonly used to query or export event logs.
Describe how log content supports account, software, and host discovery.
Explain how real time log monitoring helps an attacker evade response.
Identify the events that record log access or log export on a host.
